paper_metadata.title: OpenIE-based Approach for Knowledge Graph construction from text
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper proposes construction of knowledge graphs from English plain text using binary OpenIE relations. It combines named-entity extraction and linking, grammatical noun-phrase association, semantic-role analysis, predicate-sense linking, and n-ary RDF representation to create coherent RDF facts.

problem_addressed: Transform unstructured English text into a Knowledge Graph/RDF representation while addressing sparse or inconsistent entity linking, choosing subject/object entities in OpenIE relations, linking relation phrases to identifiers, and representing relation context that a single RDF triple would omit.

methodology.description: Execution-order pipeline: (1) acquire IT-news webpages and clean them to plain text; (2) Stanford CoreNLP performs sentence segmentation, POS tagging, constituency parsing, and filters sentences to 5–25 words with an NP–verb–NP pattern; (3) invoke DBpedia Spotlight, Babelfy, and TagMe for entity mentions and DBpedia-linked IRIs, then resolve overlaps by maximal match, choose conflicting links by majority vote, and deduplicate; (4) associate selected entities with constituency-tree noun phrases by surface-form matching; (5) extract binary relations using ClausIE; (6) run Mate-Tools SRL to match the OpenIE predicate to PropBank senses and identify Agent/A0 and Patient/A1; (7) when SRL is partial or absent, use rule-based nearest-entity and subject/object fallbacks; (8) query Premon by predicate sense to obtain an IRI; (9) create event-centred n-ary RDF/TriG named graphs with agent, patient, NP memberships, sentence provenance, and relation comment; optionally store them in a graph store.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: Uses Semantic Web RDF and named graphs; DBpedia supplies entity IRIs; PropBank predicate senses are mapped to Premon IRIs through SPARQL; Gold vocabulary represents agent/patient roles, dcterms:isPartOf represents entity membership in noun-phrase resources, and NIF preserves sentence context. It does not map predicates to a domain ontology property; it models them as event types in an n-ary representation.

input_output.input_type: English plain text extracted from IT-news webpages (with webpage HTML cleaned before processing).
input_output.input_granularity: Web documents are processed as segmented sentences; entity-linking and relation-extraction evaluations use 100 randomly selected sentences, while RDF generation uses all sentences from 605 documents.
input_output.output_representation: Event-centred n-ary RDF triples in TriG, organized in named graphs. Each event is typed with a Premon/PropBank predicate-sense IRI, linked to agent and patient NP resources, whose constituent DBpedia entities use dcterms:isPartOf; the graph retains the source sentence using NIF and relation text as rdfs:comment.

models_and_tools: ClausIE with default parameters and CC option
datasets: Author-collected IT-news webpage corpus: 605 webpages from nine RSS providers, 12,015 segmented sentences after preprocessing.
EEL/RE test sample: 100 randomly selected IT-news sentences; EEL sample averaged 24.27 words and had 614 named entities linked to DBpedia.
RDF quantitative evaluation: complete 605-document corpus / 12,015 sentences.
RDF qualitative evaluation: 50 events, each containing four triples, judged by four IT-engineering-college students.

metrics: RDF counts: entities, extracted relations, RDF-represented relations/events, RDF statements
baselines: EEL: Babelfy, DBpedia Spotlight, and TagMe individual systems.
OpenIE relation extraction: Stanford OIE and OIE4, compared with ClausIE.
RDF coherence: ablated version of the authors' system without noun-phrase/entity association.
evaluation.setting: EEL and relation extraction were manually evaluated by a human annotator against exact entity mention-plus-IRI matches and relation correctness on separately sampled 100-sentence subsets. The full corpus was used for RDF production statistics. For RDF quality, four IT-college students with at least intermediate English and familiarity with RDF roles judged 50 sampled events each; each event comprised four triples and was assessed for agent/subject, predicate, patient/object, semantic relation, and whole triple. Reported machine: 8GB RAM, Intel Core i5 2.7GHz, OS X Yosemite.

value: On 100 IT-news sentences, the EEL integration obtained P=0.8139, R=0.9643, F1=0.8827 and 731 entities; TagMe obtained F1=0.8305, Spotlight F1=0.6566, and Babelfy F1=0.6242. Spotlight had the highest precision (0.8560) but lowest recall (0.5325).
On 100 IT-news sentences, ClausIE obtained P=0.638, R=0.620, F1=0.628 for relation extraction, versus OIE4 F1=0.580 and Stanford OIE F1=0.330.
Across 12,015 sentences, the pipeline produced 103,401 linked entities, 41,190 extracted relations, 12,686 RDF-represented events/relations, and 89,486 RDF statements.

For 50 manually judged RDF events, median precision was 0.72 for subject/agent, 0.89 predicate, 0.64 object/patient, 0.82 semantic relation, and 0.51 complete triple. The NP-association ablation changed these to 0.50, 0.90, 0.46, 0.80, and 0.26, respectively.
Inter-rater Kappa was 0.4533 subject, 0.6466 predicate, 0.3133 object, 0.7000 relation, and 0.3800 triple.

value: Author-reported: combining EEL systems improves F1 relative to each individual evaluated EEL tool (0.8827 versus the best individual 0.8305).
Author-reported: noun-phrase/entity association improves judged RDF subject, object, relation, and complete-triple precision over the no-NP-association ablation.

Review-level inference: the event-centred n-ary representation retains multiple linked entities, semantic roles, original sentence context, and relation text, making provenance and contextual qualifiers more explicit than a bare binary triple.
Review-level inference: the modular pipeline permits replacement of the chosen OpenIE, EEL, SRL, or storage tool without changing the stated RDF-preparation logic.

value: Author-reported: only relations whose subject and object contain named-entity resources are represented; literal-valued RDF objects are outside the method's focus.
Author-reported: less than one third of extracted relations were represented in RDF on the full corpus (12,686 of 41,190), due to this entity-resource requirement.

Review-level inference: end-to-end quality is bounded by dependent external tools (entity linking, ClausIE, SRL, and predicate-sense mapping), so an upstream extraction or linking error can propagate into the RDF graph.

Review-level inference: heuristic fallbacks that assign nearest entities and assume subject=Agent/object=Patient when SRL is incomplete can be unreliable for syntactically complex, passive, or semantically atypical sentences.
Review-level inference: evaluation is limited to author-collected IT-news text and small manual samples; its results do not establish generality to other domains, genres, or noisy text.

Author-reported: differences in human judgment remain substantial, particularly for subject/object and complete-triple correctness (Kappa 0.4533, 0.3133, and 0.3800 respectively).

Review-level inference: robust graph construction from noisy, informal, or non-webpage text remains unresolved because the evaluated method deliberately selects well-written IT-news content and filters sentence structures.

Review-level inference: open-domain predicate alignment remains unresolved when a PropBank/Premon event type is not the same as an application-specific ontology property; this paper models the predicate as an event type rather than demonstrating domain-property alignment.
